metadata.title: Chapter 14: Active/Passive Voice (કર્તરી અને કર્મણી પ્રયોગ)
metadata.subject: Gujarati
learning_outcomes: Understand the fundamental difference between [DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ] and [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ] in Gujarati grammar.
Identify the subject, object, and verb in a Gujarati sentence.
Transform active voice sentences into passive voice correctly.
Recognize the appropriate usage of voice based on context and focus.

ai_context.learning_goal: Master sentence transformation and syntactic roles in Gujarati grammar through structured analogies and Socratic guidance.
common_misconceptions: Students often confuse the subject with the object in Gujarati sentences due to postpositions like 'એ' (ne/e).
Students think passive voice (કર્મણી) can be created without changing the verb form.

blocks.title: The Mystery of the Broken Vase
blocks.body: Imagine walking into a living room at Shine Academy and finding a shattered vase on the floor. Teacher Ramesh asks, 'Who did this?' Student Aarav steps forward and says, 'I broke the vase.' But Student Meera says, 'The vase was broken by me.' Both sentences describe the exact same event, yet they feel completely different! One puts the spotlight directly on Aarav, while the other places the broken vase center-stage. In Gujarati grammar, this magical ability to shift the spotlight is called [DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ] and [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ]. Let's unlock how Gujarati sentences rearrange themselves to change who or what is most important!

blocks.question: In the story, when Meera says 'The vase was broken by me,' where is the primary focus of the sentence?
options: On Meera, because she admitted to it
On the vase, because it is placed at the center of attention
blocks.explanation: Just like in English, passive constructions in Gujarati shift the focus from the doer of the action to the object that receives the action.

blocks.title: Concept 1: Understanding Sentence Architecture (કર્તા અને કર્મ)
blocks.body: Before we dive into voice, we must inspect the building blocks of any Gujarati sentence. Every complete sentence relies on three core pillars: the [DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા] (Subject/Doer), the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ] (Object/Receiver), and the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYA|ક્રિયાપદ] (Verb/Action). For instance, in the sentence 'રમેશે સફરજન ખાધું' (Ramesh ate an apple), Ramesh is the doer ([DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા]), the apple is what gets eaten ([DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ]), and 'ate' is the action ([DICT_GUJ_KRIYA|ક્રિયાપદ]). In Gujarati, the relationship between these three components dictates whether our sentence is active or passive. Understanding who does the action and who receives it is the master key to unlocking advanced language fluency.

blocks.title: The Spotlight Analogy
blocks.body: Think of a Gujarati sentence as a theater stage. The [DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા] is the superstar actor, and the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ] is the special prop. In active voice, the spotlight shines brightly on the actor. In passive voice, the stage crew pivots the spotlight so it glares directly on the prop!

blocks.front: What is 'કર્તા' (Karta) in a Gujarati sentence?
blocks.back: The Subject or the 'doer' of the action.

blocks.front: What is 'કર્મ' (Karma) in a Gujarati sentence?
blocks.back: The Object or the receiver of the action.

blocks.title: Concept 2: The Power of Active Voice ([DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ])
blocks.body: Let's explore the most natural and frequently used sentence structure in Gujarati: [DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ] (Active Voice). In this structure, the verb agrees in gender, number, and person directly with the [DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા] (Subject). For example: 'બાળકે ચોપડી વાંચી' (The child read a book). Notice how the verb 'વાંચી' aligns with 'બાળક'. The subject takes the main responsibility for the action. Active voice is direct, energetic, and leaves no doubt about who is performing the task. It is the default mode of human communication, making conversations punchy and clear.

blocks.question: In the sentence 'ગીતાએ ગીત ગાયું' (Geeta sang a song), which word is the [DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા]?
blocks.explanation: ગીતાએ is the doer of the action (the subject), making this an active sentence.

blocks.title: Concept 3: Shifting to Passive Voice ([DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ])
blocks.body: Now let's enter the realm of [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ] (Passive Voice). When do we use it? Often when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when we want to emphasize the object ([DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ]). In Gujarati, transforming a sentence into passive voice requires specific structural changes: 1) The subject ([DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા]) takes a postposition like 'થી' (by/from) or 'દ્વારા' (through). 2) The verb agrees with the object ([DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ]) in gender and number, rather than the subject. For instance, active 'અમે કેરી ખાધી' becomes passive 'અમારાથી કેરી ખાધી ગઈ' (The mango was eaten by us). Notice how the verb now follows the object 'કેરી'.

blocks.title: Spotting the 'થી' Clue
blocks.body: A foolproof way to spot a [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ] sentence in Gujarati is to look for the particle 'થી' attached to the subject (e.g., 'બાળકથી', 'રામથી', 'તેમનાથી'), paired with a modified ending on the verb.

blocks.question: Which of the following sentences is in [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ] (Passive Voice)?
blocks.explanation: વિદ્યાર્થીથી પાઠ ભણાયો uses the passive marker 'થી' and the verb aligns with the object 'પાઠ'.

blocks.title: Concept 4: Step-by-Step Transformation Rules
blocks.body:
Transforming sentences is an art that requires precision. Let's break down the exact mathematical recipe for converting Active ([DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ]) to Passive ([DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ]): 

Step 1: Identify the [DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા] and append 'થી' to it.
Step 2: Identify the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ] and ensure it remains the focal point.
Step 3: Adjust the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYA|ક્રિયાપદ] so its gender and number match the object, adding auxiliary endings like 'વાયું', 'ગયું', or modifying the root verb (e.g., લખવું -> લખાયું).

Let's test this with 'છોકરાએ પત્ર લખ્યો' (The boy wrote a letter). Step 1: છોકરાથી. Step 2: પત્ર. Step 3: લખાયો. Result: 'છોકરાથી પત્ર લખાયો'.

blocks.front: What suffix is typically added to the subject when converting an active Gujarati sentence to passive?

blocks.question: Convert 'અધ્યાપકે પુસ્તક વાંચ્યું' into passive voice.
blocks.explanation: The subject gets 'થી' (અધ્યાપકથી) and the verb adapts to the object (પુસ્તક વાંચાયું).

blocks.title: Concept 5: Why and When Do We Switch Voices?
blocks.body: Language is not just about rules; it is about expression. Why would a writer choose [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ] over [DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ]? First, when the doer is unknown or irrelevant (e.g., 'બારીનો કાચ તૂટી ગયો' - The window glass got broken, without blaming anyone specifically). Second, in formal, legal, or official Gujarati writing, passive voice sounds objective and polite. Third, it avoids taking personal credit or blame. Mastering both voices gives you stylistic flexibility, allowing you to control the exact mood and emphasis of your Gujarati prose.

blocks.title: The 'Accident' Test
blocks.body: Notice how in real life, when we want to sound less blameworthy for an accident (like spilling milk or breaking a toy), we naturally shift to passive voice ('દૂધ ઢોળાઈ ગયું' - Milk got spilled, instead of 'મેં દૂધ ઢોળ્યું' - I spilled milk). Grammar reflects human psychology!

blocks.question: Which sentence best hides or minimizes the identity of the person who committed the action?
blocks.explanation: 'ચોરી થઈ ગઈ' (The theft happened) completely removes the doer, showcasing how passive constructions can omit agents entirely.

blocks.front: True or False: In Gujarati passive voice, the verb agrees with the subject.
blocks.back: False! The verb agrees with the object (કર્મ) in gender and number.

blocks.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
blocks.body: Even advanced learners stumble upon subtle traps when dealing with Gujarati voice transformation. Pitfall 1: Changing tense accidentally. If the active sentence is in past tense ('ખાધું'), the passive sentence must also reflect the past time frame ('ખાધું ગયું' or 'ખાધુરું'). Pitfall 2: Forgetting gender agreement. In Gujarati, nouns have genders (Masculine, Feminine, Neuter). If the object is feminine (e.g., 'ચોપડી'), the passive verb must match it ('ચોપડી વંચાઈ', not 'વંચાયો'). Keeping a sharp eye on noun genders is crucial for flawless Gujarati grammar.

blocks.question: If the object 'શાકભાજી' (vegetables - plural/neuter context) is used in a passive sentence, how should the verb conclude?
blocks.explanation: Matching the object's plural/neuter form correctly ensures grammatical harmony.

blocks.title: Gender Check Drill
blocks.body: Before writing your final passive verb, ask yourself: Is the object male, female, or neuter? Say the object aloud with its gender tag, then select the matching verb ending!

blocks.title: Summary of Shine Academy's Grammar Masterclass
blocks.body: We have journeyed from the basics of sentence anatomy to the subtle art of voice shifting. [DICT_GUJ_KARTARI|કર્તરી પ્રયોગ] puts the [DICT_GUJ_KARTA|કર્તા] (Subject) in the driver's seat, making sentences direct and dynamic. [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|કર્મણી પ્રયોગ] hands the steering wheel to the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|કર્મ] (Object), using the postposition 'થી' and altering the verb for elegance, objectivity, or shifting emphasis. Practice these rules daily, and your Gujarati writing will shine with clarity and professional polish!

blocks.question: What is the primary marker that connects the subject in a passive Gujarati sentence?
blocks.explanation: 'થી' is the standard instrumental postposition used in passive constructions in Gujarati.
